claims.text: Verbatim: '(e)(1) The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis. (2) If the Secretary exercises the authority provided under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.'

The waiver authority is vested in the Secretary of Defense personally and is conditioned only on the Secretary's own determination of adverse national security effect; the statute prescribes no finding of fact, no time limit, no periodic re-justification, and no congressional ability to disapprove.

Subsection (e) was in the section as originally enacted by Pub. L. 100-180 sec. 1132(a)(1) (4 Dec 1987) and has never been amended: the 2001, 1999, 1996 and 1990 amendment notes in the GPO text touch only subsecs. (a)(1), (c), (f) and (g). The waiver language of 1987 is the language in force today.

Because (e)(1) reaches only 'any requirement ... that certain information be included in a report,' a plain reading is that the Secretary may strip content out of the reports but may not skip the (f) 30-day pre-initiation notification of the program's existence. A program whose existence was never notified to the defense committees at all would therefore not be a lawfully 'waived' SAP under section 119 but an unreported one. Reasoning stated from the text of (e)(1) and (f).

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1): 'The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.'

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2): the Secretary 'shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.'
The waiver authority extends only to subsections (a), (b) and (c); the 30-day pre-initiation notice requirement of subsection (f) is not waivable on the face of the statute.
Section 119(e) imposes no requirement to maintain, publish or report a register of waivers exercised.

Read literally, 119(g) names six bodies - Senate Armed Services, Senate Appropriations, the Defense Subcommittee of Senate Appropriations, and the three House counterparts - so 'the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' is up to twelve members, not eight. The conventional 'Gang of Eight' framing for defense waived programs counts only the four parent committees. Reasoning: statutory text versus practice convention.

desc: Subsection (e) is the hinge of this entire board. In two paragraphs it converts the full committee reporting regime of section 119 into a briefing for a handful of individuals. Paragraph (1): 'The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.' Paragraph (2): 'If the Secretary exercises the authority provided under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' Four features matter. First, the waiver is unilateral - no committee concurrence, no ISOO review, no judicial test; the sole standard is the Secretary's own determination. Second, the waiver reaches subsections (a), (b) and (c) - the annual report, the new-program notice and the declassification notice - but not subsection (f), so the 30-day pre-initiation notice to the committees survives on paper. Third, the information does not vanish: it goes to named leaders, which is why programs run under a section 119(e) waiver are called 'waived' programs and are informally said to be briefed to a 'Gang of Eight'. Fourth, and decisively, section 119(e) contains no audit trail requirement - no register of waivers exercised, no annual accounting of how many waivers are outstanding, no requirement that the waived program appear anywhere in an unclassified count. The number of waived DoD special access programs currently in existence has never been published.

entityInfo.desc: The hinge, stated as plainly as it can be. A witness alleging that Congress was not told about a program is usually assumed to be alleging a crime. Under 10 U.S.C. 119(e) that assumption is wrong. The Secretary of Defense may lawfully decide, case by case, that telling the defense committees something would adversely affect national security, and thereupon tell only the chairman and ranking minority member of each committee instead. There is no committee veto, no ISOO concurrence, no court, no register of waivers, no expiry, no periodic requirement to widen access, and no penalty. Compare the covert action regime, which is normally described as the most secretive corner of American government: under 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B), when access to a finding is limited to the Gang of Eight, the President must within 180 days either open it to all members of the intelligence committees or file a further written statement of reasons. A waived special access program has no such clock. That comparison is the single most useful fact this domain contributes to the board: the mechanism at the centre of the Grusch allegations is lawful, is older than the allegation, is weaker than the covert action rule it is usually compared to, and leaves an auditable paper trail in exactly two places - the Secretary's waiver determinations, and the Senior Review Group's annual review of all waived programs.
